lines.note: The opening uelo finishes a word from the preceding page. Uma ga ke wo kayuru describes the horse changing its coat; the Portuguese mudar continues on the next row.
Os cabelos o caualo completes the description of shedding or changing the coat. Uma wo tsukuroo introduces tending or treating the horse, explained immediately below.
The treatment includes bleeding the horse. The scan supports caualo rather than OCR cauulo; Vma- begins the next example and remains divided at the printed line end.

runs.text: Dar de eſporas ao caualo, ou

lines.note: Uma wo hayamuru means making the horse go faster. The gloss specifies applying the spurs, followed by a second paraphrase on the next row.
Fazelo ir de preßa completes the acceleration gloss. Uma wo tatsuru then introduces putting the horse up or stabling it; Por belongs to that new explanation.
The stable completes the preceding example. Uma wo hadaquru begins the following grooming expression; its final syllable continues below.
Ru completes hadaquru, and coxirayuru is an alternative expression introduced by Latin l. Almofaçar identifies the action as curry-combing or grooming the horse.
Uma ga agaru describes a horse rearing. The Portuguese phrase porse o caualo em gemeas is divided ge-/meas across the physical rows.
Meas completes the rearing description. Uma ga tsuke sumoo introduces a horse resisting its rider mounting; the gloss begins repugnar across the line break.

runs.text: nar o caualo quando quer ſubir o caualeiro che-

lines.note: The horse resists when the rider tries to mount. Che- begins chegandose, describing how it crowds the rider in the next row.

runs.text: gandoſe muito, & afastando ao que quer ca-

lines.note: Gandose completes chegandose: the horse comes too close and drives away the person trying to mount. The scan supports o in gandoſe and the f of afastando; the short-s st spelling is retained rather than normalizing this difficult ligature.
Ualgar completes caualgar. Tsuqeuma names a horse with this obstructive habit, and its Portuguese explanation continues below.
After finishing the description of that habit, uma ga noquru means the horse moves away. Afaſ continues as tarſe on the next row; no terminal hyphen is supplied without visible ink.

runs.text: tarſe o caualo pera não deixar ſubir o caualeiro.

lines.note: The horse withdraws so that the rider cannot get on. This completes afastarse and explains the preceding noquru example.

Noqevma names a horse with the just-described habit of backing away from a would-be rider. The scan supplies the omitted paragraph sign and an upright v in the compound; the unpunctuated line ending is retained.
Uma ga soramu introduces raising and tossing the head, with the intended consequence for the rider explained in the next two rows.

runs.text: cabeça, & abanala pera derrubar o que vai em

lines.note: The horse raises and shakes its head to throw the person riding it. The phrase em cima continues on the following physical row.
Cima completes the description of the mounted rider. Uma ga uchikomu, alternatively uchikonde yuku across the next row, describes another movement used to unseat him.

runs.text: Ir o caualo com a cabeça entras

lines.note: De yuqu completes uchikonde yuku. The Portuguese says the horse goes with its head between its legs; the scan supports Ir and the article a before cabeça rather than OCR Er and an omitted article.

runs.text: pernas pera derrubar o que vai em cima.

lines.note: The horse puts its head between its legs to throw the rider. This closes the long series of horse-handling examples before the new calendrical sense of uma.

runs.text: Hum dos animaes por onde os Iapões cõ

lines.note: Uma is now the Horse of the calendrical animal cycle. Onde is worn but its rounded initial and the following counting explanation support it over OCR cnde; cõ continues into tão below without expanding the abbreviation.
The animals are used to count years and hours. Uma no koku is the Horse hour; the print has horas, not OCR boras, and the next row gives its approximate limits.

runs.text: Das 11. atè ao meo dia, & mais.

lines.note: The Horse hour runs from eleven to noon and beyond in the printed explanation. The scan reads 11., ao meo dia, and & mais; the OCR E/r fragment was a failed recognition of the number.

runs.text: Coco de tomar agoa pera lauar o

lines.note: Umabishaku is a coconut-shell dipper used to take water for washing a horse. The definition supplies its function without requiring a specific vessel shape beyond coco.
Caualo completes the purpose of the dipper: washing the horse. This short line belongs to the preceding entry.

Umabune is the horse's manger. Enlargement supports the ending une rather than OCR uite, while the b is heavily abraded. The supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho (Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), consulted after the independent reading, corroborates Vmabune; this remains a qualified scan reading, not a copied diplomatic authority.
Umakata is the person who handles or transports goods with horses, matched by almocreue. The Portuguese is an occupational noun, not an adjective describing a horse.

runs.text: Ser o caualo brioſo, ou que logo

lines.note: Umadaqei describes a spirited horse. Logo, visible at the end of the line, introduces its immediate reaction on seeing other horses; OCR hoeo was not a coherent gloss.

runs.text: ſe encreſpa, ou rincha vendo a outros. ¶

lines.note: The horse bristles or neighs on seeing others. The damaged but legible encreſpa restores the Portuguese verb; V- begins the Japanese example on the next indented row.
V- plus madaqei forms the same adjective as the headword, followed by uma ja: it is a spirited horse. The scan supports madaqei vmagia rather than OCR madiqeivmagia.
Umafada names a thick, soft mat placed beneath a saddle. Esteira is damaged in the middle but the surviving letters and the following placement support the mat sense rather than OCR Esioro.

runs.text: de baixo da ſela do caualo.

lines.note: De baixo da sela do caualo completes the saddle-pad definition. The visible word division de baixo is retained.

runs.text: Almocreue, ou moço que leua o

lines.note: Umahiki is a horse-leader or attendant, compared with an almocreue. The visible initial V and the occupational gloss correct OCR Nmafiqi and Al nocreue; the sentence continues with the means of leading.

runs.text: caualo pollo cabreſto, ou pollas rideas.

lines.note: The attendant leads the horse by its halter or reins. Caualo replaces the OCR vowel error cauulo; the worn spelling rideas is retained.

runs.text: O ir pella posta, ou correndo a ca-

lines.note: Umagaqe denotes riding post or going at speed on horseback. The scan has the initial V omitted by OCR and the Portuguese phrase O ir pella posta, ou correndo.
Ualo completes caualo. Umagaqete yuku is the corresponding verbal expression; Idem repeats the meaning, and Mas begins a usage qualification.
The expression is said not to be very commonly used. The negative is printed não, not the OCR nũo, and the historical form vſado is retained.
Umaguinu is the horse's blanket. The concise gloss manta do caualo provides the whole meaning of this entry.

runs.text: Pentem com que penteão a coma

lines.note: Umaguxi is a comb used to groom the mane. The Portuguese coma refers to the horse's mane; it is not a person's hair in this context.
Do caualo completes the mane-comb definition, specifying the animal. This short continuation is distinct from the adjective umai below.
Umai means pleasant-tasting or savoury, matching gostoſa and ſabroſa. The scan contains Vmai without the spurious n introduced by OCR.
Umaſi is the corresponding adjective in its -shi form, sharing the preceding definition of something tasty. It occupies its own indented line and has no separately repeated Portuguese gloss.
Vmǒ is the contracted adverbial form of the tasty adjective, grouped with umai and umashi. The visible caron belongs to o; the OCR extra na is absent.

Vmaſacari is followed by Melius and the preferred form Vmazacari, then a definition of a mudhole. The scan supports c and the complete Melius. The tall glyph is retained as ſ: it lacks the right crossbar of nearby f types. The supplied NINJAL index instead gives Vmajacari and reports an apparent f interpreted as an inverted j; that editorial interpretation is not silently substituted for this copy's ambiguous glyph.

runs.text: atoleiro por onde cuſtumão paßar os caualos dei

lines.note: The mudhole is a place habitually crossed by horses. Cuſtumão has a visible t absent from the OCR; dei continues into xãdo below without adding an unprinted line-end hyphen.

runs.text: xãdo huas couas, ou poças em que todos metẽ

lines.note: Dei followed by xãdo explains that the horses leave hollows or puddles into which they put their feet, continued at the top of column 2. The scan supports xãdo and poças; the abraded huas is retained without adding an uncertain nasal mark.

runs.text: os pès ſacudindo a lama, ou agoa.

lines.note: The horses put their feet into the hollows, splashing mud or water. This completes Vmaſacari from the preceding column; the scan separates ſacudindo a, unlike the OCR run-together form.
Uma ikada is a raft for ferrying horses. The visibly separate Vma icada is preserved even though the following example writes the compound together.
Umaikada wo kumu means constructing or assembling such a raft. The Portuguese repeats the same object, retaining the abbreviation tilde in iãgada.
Uma mawarishu denotes respected retainers serving a lord or commander. The gloss begins their rank comparison, continued on the next row.

runs.text: nhor, ou capitão que ſão mais que pagens.

lines.note: These attendants are ranked above pages. Senhor is divided ſe-/nhor across the physical rows; the comparison is social rank, not the number of servants.

runs.text: Soldados de caualo, ou que vão

lines.note: Umamusha are mounted soldiers. Soldados has a damaged d but is a single Portuguese word; the OCR split Sol lados is unsupported.
A caualo completes the alternative explanation: soldiers who go on horseback. It remains a short continuation of umamusha.

runs.text: Caualeiro, ou o que vai a caualo,

lines.note: Umanori means a rider, someone on horseback. The Portuguese continues with a further evaluative sense on the next row.
Bom caualeiro adds the sense of a skilled rider. The definition thus covers both a rider generally and a good horseman.

runs.text: Os que vão a caualo, ou gen-

lines.note: Umanori no shu refers collectively to people on horseback or mounted troops. The Portuguese gente is divided gen-/te at the line break.
Te completes gente de caualo, the mounted group. This closes the collective entry before the dust raised by horses is introduced.
Umagemuri is dust raised by many horses. The Portuguese caualos continues onto the next physical row.
The horses are travelling together. Umagemuri wo tatete tatakoo begins the example of fighting while raising clouds of horse-dust, with tatete divided at ta-.
Tete completes tatete before tatacǒ, fighting. The scan supports final e rather than OCR teto; the Portuguese emphasizes the noise and commotion of battle.
Poeira completes the battle gloss: great noise and dust. The visible second vowel is e, correcting OCR pocira.
Umare is the noun for birth. The worn Portuguese Nacimento fits the noun and the adjacent verb nacer; its c is faint, but there is no basis for retaining OCR Narimento.
Umare, umaruru, umareta gives the verb for being born, paired with Portuguese nacer. The historical principal forms remain as printed rather than being converted to modern umareru.
Umareai names agreement or compatibility between people in their inborn nature. The visible e in the headword replaces OCR c, and the gloss continues natureza below.
Reza completes natureza, followed by condição: the compatibility is of nature or disposition. The scan supports condição without the spurious extra l in OCR condlição.
The verb umareai means being born under a particular conjunction or at a particular time. Its abbreviated principal parts ǒ and ǒta are retained, including the carons.

runs.text: gum planeta, ou em algum tempo notauel. Vt,

lines.note: The definition refers to a planet's conjunction or another notable time. Vt introduces a religious example of fortunate timing at birth.

Go-oqite no hiromaru jibun ni umareau means happening to be born when the divine law is spreading, as the Portuguese explains. The unusual printed vmarevǒ is retained; it should not be regularized from the headword's abbreviated ǒ. The stroke between e and ǒ is partly abraded, so the retained v remains uncertain.

runs.text: Acertar de nacer em tẽpo que a ley de Deos ſe

lines.note: The translation describes being born during the dissemination of the law of God. Tẽpo preserves the abbreviation tilde, while ley and Deos retain the source spelling.
Diuulga completes the statement that God's law is becoming known. It is a continuation of the example, not a new headword.
Umarecauari means being born again or differently. The principal form ru is fully visible, correcting the OCR truncated r; the definition continues below.

runs.text: vez differente do que era, ou nacer em outra

lines.note: Rebirth is described as becoming different from what one was or being born in another form. The phrase em outra introduces figura on the following row.

Figura and ſuſtancia complete the first rebirth sense. The entry then introduces a regional use in Ximo, with the place name divided Xi-/mo across the physical rows; its capital X is visible. The lowercase i and mo are italic, while the less secure upright-looking X retains the baseline font treatment.

runs.text: mo, nacer ſomenos, ou inferior nos eſpiritos,

lines.note: Mo completes Ximo. In that region the word can mean being born inferior in spirit or abilities; the comparison with the father continues below. The second pass identified the visible right crossbar in inferior, correcting OCR inſerior.

runs.text: & partes ao pay. No Cami ſe diz

lines.note: The child is inferior to the father in qualities. The Cami usage is then given as umare votoru across two lines; Vmare contains no extra n despite the OCR Vmnare.
Votoru completes umare votoru, the contrasting regional expression for being born inferior. It is the quoted expression governed by No Cami se diz above.

runs.text: Nacido de pouco, ou logo em

lines.note: Umaredachi means newly born or immediately upon birth. The two Portuguese paraphrases continue with nacendo on the next row.
Nacendo completes logo em nacendo. Umaredachini yagate fito-ni begins an example of handing the newborn to another person to be raised.
Ni yashinawaseta completes the causative example: having someone else raise the newborn. The Portuguese begins the explicit temporal paraphrase, immediately after birth.

runs.text: o dei a criar a outro. ¶

lines.note: The translation says I gave the child to another to raise. Umaredachino then starts a second expression, modifying ko on the following line.
Ko completes umaredachi no ko, a recently born child. The Portuguese criança nacida de pouco gives that same meaning directly.

runs.text: O nacer outra vez neſte mun-

lines.note: Umaregawari is rebirth into this world. The scan includes neſte before the divided mundo, correcting the OCR omission of n in eſte.

runs.text: do em differente figura, ou ſuſtancia ſegundo

lines.note: The reborn being has a different form or substance. The gloss is reporting a belief, with ſegundo introducing its attribution below. The final a of ſuſtancia is worn; its small right foot favors a over OCR o, but this remains a qualified a/o reading.

runs.text: imaginão os gentios, como ſe v. g. Xaca

lines.note: The compilers attribute this belief to gentios and illustrate it with Shaka, printed Xaca. The visible i restores gentios; the statement is the source's account of rebirth rather than an editorial assertion of its truth.

runs.text: tornaße agora a nacer transformado em al-

lines.note: The hypothetical example has Shaka born again and transformed. Al- begins algum on the following row; the historical tornaße spelling is preserved.
Gum completes algum Bonzo: the rebirth would be as a Buddhist monk. Bonzo is the Portuguese term in the explanation, not a separately quoted Japanese headword.

runs.text: O degenerar, ou não ſair à

lines.note: Umaregayeri describes degeneration or failure to take after the parents. The OCR extra n after não is stray ink; the line-final à has a visible accent and introduces caſta below.
The child does not match the parents' stock or qualities. Umaregayerini natta is the example; its repeated gayeri has e, not the OCR gayori, and the terminal mark is read as a period.

runs.text: Ficar algum filho de homem, ou de animal in-

lines.note: The translation concerns the offspring of either a human or another animal becoming inferior. In- begins inferior at the physical line end.
Ferior aos pays completes inferior to the parents. This closes the negative contrast before the next entry describes a child surpassing them.
Umaremaxi is being born with an advantage or superior qualities. Its -ita principal form is retained as historical morphology, and the gloss continues the comparison below.

runs.text: milhor q̃ outro como o filho milhor que o pay,

lines.note: The example is a son better than his father. Milhor and the abbreviated q̃ are preserved as printed, and the comma continues into &c. below.

The previously omitted &c. finishes the comparison of a child with the father. The signature and catchword sharing this baseline are recorded separately as page furniture, so neither is inserted into the running definition.
Anticipates Vmareqi at the opening of f538. The terminal mark is weak and affected by the nearby border; Vmare- is retained as the usable reading rather than the OCR Vmarea.
